title: Giant Cell Arteritis vs Takayasu Arteritis: Age, Markers and the Negative Biopsy
summary: Sort the two large-vessel vasculitides by age, learn how sensitive ESR and CRP really are in giant cell arteritis, and see why a negative temporal artery biopsy does not exclude the disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 54 Hit 7 (giant cell arteritis: age, ESR/CRP sensitivity, biopsy false negatives), Hit 15 (Takayasu vs GCA by age) and Trap 4 (negative temporal artery biopsy), checked against Kermani 2012 (read via a page-fetch tool), van der Geest 2020, Duftner 2018, Maz 2021 (ACR/VF guideline; read via a page-fetch tool, first part of the page only), Hwang 2026, Tecer 2025 and Russo 2018. Three qualifications: Kermani 2012 reports the 4% double-normal figure in patients not on glucocorticoids (10.2% including treated patients; register flag rv-gca-normal-markers-steroids); Duftner 2018 reports biopsy false negatives in up to 61% versus a clinical diagnosis, far above the reviewer’s “up to 15%” (register flag rv-gca-tab-false-negative-rate); and the 2022 ACR/EULAR Takayasu criteria use age ≤60 at diagnosis (previously onset ≤40), not the reviewer’s “<50” (register flag rv-takayasu-age-cutoff). Not taught as fact: the reviewer’s “44% of quiet Takayasu patients have active arteritis on biopsy” (only the qualitative finding is taught), “Scandinavian whites”, the >20/100,000 Scandinavian incidence, and the advice never to stop steroids for a negative biopsy (sources read describe contralateral biopsy and imaging, not a stop/continue rule). The 2022 criteria papers themselves were not read (not open access); their entry rules are taken from Hwang 2026, Molina-Collada 2023 and Tecer 2025.

objectives: Distinguish giant cell arteritis from Takayasu arteritis by age and sex, and state the 2022 classification entry rules.
Interpret ESR and CRP in suspected giant cell arteritis, including their limited specificity and the rare double-normal case.
Explain why a negative temporal artery biopsy does not exclude giant cell arteritis, and name the next steps the 2021 guideline describes.

scenes.title: Two arteritis requests, one shortcut
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two requests arrive. Patient 1: a 72-year-old woman with a new temporal headache and jaw claudication; ESR and CRP are both within the reference range, and a left temporal artery biopsy is reported negative. Patient 2: a 24-year-old woman with arm claudication and a weak radial pulse. A sticky note on patient 1 reads: “Normal markers, negative biopsy: GCA ruled out?”

cues.text: Two requests arrive. A seventy-two-year-old woman has a new temporal headache and jaw pain on chewing. Her ESR and CRP are normal, and one temporal artery biopsy is negative.
A twenty-four-year-old woman has arm pain on exertion and a weak pulse at the wrist.
Someone has written on the first request: normal markers, negative biopsy, giant cell arteritis ruled out. Is it?

props.label: Normal markers + negative biopsy = ruled out?

scenes.title: Two large-vessel diseases on an age axis
scenes.altText: Schematic age axis from 0 to 90 years. Giant cell arteritis (GCA) card: age 50 or over at diagnosis is an absolute entry requirement in the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria; incidence peaks at 70–79 years; highest incidence in Scandinavia, more common in people of Northern European descent. Takayasu arteritis (TAK) card: onset typically 10–40 years; 80–90% of patients are women; more prevalent in Asia; the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria require age 60 or under at diagnosis plus imaging evidence of vasculitis (the 1990 criteria used onset at 40 or under). Temporal artery biopsy has no role in diagnosing TAK.

cues.text: Giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis both inflame the aorta and its large branches. Age is the first sorting question.

Giant cell arteritis occurs almost only at fifty or older, with a peak in the seventies. Incidence is highest in Scandinavia. The 2022 classification criteria make age fifty or over an entry requirement.

Takayasu arteritis usually begins between ten and forty, and eighty to ninety percent of patients are women. The 2022 criteria require age sixty or under at diagnosis plus imaging evidence of vasculitis. The 1990 criteria used forty.
Temporal artery biopsy belongs to giant cell arteritis. It has no role in diagnosing Takayasu arteritis, which rests on imaging.

props.label: Temporal artery biopsy: GCA only · TAK = imaging

scenes.title: ESR and CRP: sensitive, not definitive
scenes.altText: Two data cards. Kermani 2012 (Mayo Clinic, biopsies 2000–2008; 177 biopsy-positive GCA): elevated ESR had a sensitivity of 84.1% and elevated CRP 86.9% for a positive biopsy; 7 patients (4%) had both normal at diagnosis even without glucocorticoid use (18 patients, 10.2%, had both normal when those already on glucocorticoids are included). van der Geest 2020 meta-analysis: elevated CRP pooled sensitivity about 87% with specificity about 31%; elevated ESR about 83% sensitivity, 34% specificity. Conclusion card: no single clinical or laboratory feature rules GCA in or out; imaging and/or biopsy are needed.

cues.text: Raised inflammatory markers are common in giant cell arteritis. In a Mayo Clinic series, an elevated ESR had a sensitivity of about eighty-four percent and an elevated CRP about eighty-seven percent for a positive biopsy.
But four percent of biopsy-proven patients had both ESR and CRP normal at diagnosis without any glucocorticoid treatment. Normal markers lower suspicion; they do not exclude the disease.
A 2020 meta-analysis found an elevated CRP about eighty-seven percent sensitive but only about thirty-one percent specific. Many people without giant cell arteritis also have raised markers.
The authors concluded that no single clinical or laboratory feature rules giant cell arteritis in or out. Imaging, biopsy, or both are needed.

props.title: No single feature rules GCA in or out

scenes.title: Why a negative biopsy can miss the disease
scenes.altText: Schematic temporal artery with patchy (segmental) inflamed segments and a short biopsy window that falls between them. Cards: biopsy is highly specific but lacks sensitivity — false negatives in up to 61% of patients compared with a clinical diagnosis (EULAR imaging review 2018). ACR/VF 2021: GCA is focal and segmental, so a segment longer than 1 cm is preferred; biopsy within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids; a contralateral biopsy is appropriate if the first is negative; large-vessel imaging can add evidence when the diagnosis is uncertain after negative biopsies. Temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) is more sensitive than biopsy for a clinical diagnosis. Hook answers: patient 1 is not ruled out; patient 2 points to Takayasu arteritis and needs vascular imaging.

cues.text: Giant cell arteritis is focal and segmental. Inflamed stretches alternate with normal wall, so a short biopsy can fall between them.
Biopsy is highly specific, but a 2018 review found false negatives in up to sixty-one percent of patients when compared with a clinical diagnosis.

The 2021 American guideline prefers a segment longer than one centimetre, taken within two weeks of starting glucocorticoids. If one side is negative, the other side can be biopsied, and large-vessel imaging can add evidence. Ultrasound for a halo sign is more sensitive than biopsy for a clinical diagnosis.
Back to the hook. The seventy-two-year-old is not ruled out: her story still fits. The twenty-four-year-old points to Takayasu arteritis, which needs vascular imaging, not a temporal biopsy.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A negative temporal artery biopsy excludes GCA” (✓ the disease is segmental; false negatives are common; a contralateral biopsy or imaging can follow); “Normal ESR and CRP exclude GCA” (✓ 4% of biopsy-proven cases had both normal without glucocorticoid use); “Clinically quiet Takayasu means no active arteritis” (✓ pathological studies have found arterial inflammation in clinically inactive disease, and about one third of patients have no raised markers at presentation).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative temporal biopsy excludes giant cell arteritis. No: the disease skips segments, and false negatives are common.
Trap two: a normal ESR and CRP exclude giant cell arteritis. No: four percent of biopsy-proven patients had both normal, even without steroids.
Trap three: clinically quiet Takayasu means no active arteritis. No: pathology has shown arterial inflammation in clinically inactive disease.

props.title: ✗ “Negative biopsy excludes GCA.”
lines: ✓ Segmental disease; false negatives are common

props.title: ✗ “Normal ESR and CRP exclude GCA.”
lines: ✓ 4% of proven cases: both normal, untreated

props.title: ✗ “Quiet Takayasu = no active arteritis.”
lines: ✓ Inflammation found in clinically inactive disease

scenes.title: Grandparent, young woman, keyhole
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “GCA is the Grandparent’s arteritis (50 or over); Takayasu is the young woman’s arteritis; the biopsy is a keyhole — seeing an empty room through one keyhole does not prove the house is empty.” Tokens: grandparent = GCA ≥50 · young woman = Takayasu · keyhole = biopsy. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: giant cell arteritis is the grandparent’s arteritis, fifty or older. Takayasu is the young woman’s arteritis. The biopsy is a keyhole: an empty view through one keyhole does not prove the house is empty.

Where it breaks: the 2022 Takayasu criteria accept diagnosis up to age sixty, and men get it too; age cut-offs are classification rules, not diagnostic tests; and some authors see the two diseases as one overlapping spectrum.

lines: TAK criteria accept age ≤ 60; men too

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “GCA: age 50 or over · Takayasu: usually young women, imaging-based”, “Normal ESR/CRP or one negative biopsy does not exclude GCA”.

cues.text: Giant cell arteritis affects people aged fifty or over and Takayasu arteritis mostly young women, and in suspected giant cell arteritis neither normal inflammatory markers nor a single negative temporal artery biopsy excludes the disease.

props.label: GCA ≥ 50 · Takayasu: mostly young women, imaging
Normal ESR/CRP or one negative biopsy ≠ GCA excluded

explanation.what: Plain language: two diseases inflame the body’s biggest arteries. Giant cell arteritis affects older people and often the arteries of the head; Takayasu arteritis mostly affects young women and the aorta and its branches. Blood inflammation tests and a small artery biopsy help, but each can miss giant cell arteritis. Scientific terms: large-vessel vasculitis, giant cell arteritis (GCA), Takayasu arteritis (TAK), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), temporal artery biopsy (TAB), focal and segmental involvement, halo sign, 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria.
explanation.why: GCA involves the artery in patches, so a short biopsy may sample normal wall; the 2021 guideline also notes that changes are more likely to be detected when the biopsy is taken within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids. Inflammatory markers rise in most patients but also in many other conditions, so they are sensitive but not specific, and a few biopsy-proven patients have both normal.
explanation.measure: GCA: age ≥50 at diagnosis (2022 entry rule); peak 70–79 years. Kermani 2012: raised ESR 84.1%, raised CRP 86.9% sensitive for a positive biopsy; 4% had both normal without glucocorticoid use, 10.2% including treated patients (normal ESR ≤22 mm/h men, ≤29 mm/h women; CRP ≤8 mg/L). Meta-analysis: raised CRP ~87% sensitive, ~31% specific. TAB false negatives up to 61% versus clinical diagnosis. ACR/VF 2021: segment >1 cm; biopsy within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids; contralateral biopsy or large-vessel imaging if negative. TAK: onset usually 10–40, 80–90% women; 2022 criteria: age ≤60 at diagnosis plus imaging evidence (1990: onset ≤40).
explanation.differs: GCA (≥50, Northern European/Scandinavian, TAB and temporal ultrasound useful) vs TAK (young, mostly women, more common in Asia, diagnosed by imaging; TAB has no role). Sensitivity (markers usually raised) vs specificity (markers also raised in other illness).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: classify a patient by age as GCA or TAK, recognise that normal ESR/CRP or a negative biopsy does not exclude GCA, and choose the next step after a negative unilateral biopsy.

mnemonic.text: GCA is the Grandparent’s arteritis (50 or over); Takayasu is the young woman’s arteritis; the biopsy is a keyhole — an empty view through one keyhole does not prove the house is empty.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each disease to its age group and reminds that a negative biopsy samples only part of a patchy artery.
mnemonic.limitation: The 2022 Takayasu criteria accept diagnosis up to age 60 and men are affected too; age cut-offs are classification rules, not diagnostic tests; some authors regard GCA and Takayasu as an overlapping spectrum.

analogyLimitations: Sensitivity figures come from one cohort and one meta-analysis; values vary with population and reference standard.
takeaway: Giant cell arteritis affects people aged fifty or over and Takayasu arteritis mostly young women, and in suspected giant cell arteritis neither normal inflammatory markers nor a single negative temporal artery biopsy excludes the disease.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has new temporal headache and jaw claudication. Her ESR and CRP are within the reference range, and a left temporal artery biopsy shows no arteritis. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: GCA is not excluded; a contralateral biopsy or vascular imaging can be considered
options.rationale: Correct. GCA is segmental, biopsy false negatives are common, and about 4% of biopsy-proven patients had both ESR and CRP normal even without glucocorticoid use. The 2021 ACR/VF guideline describes contralateral biopsy and large-vessel imaging after a negative biopsy.

options.text: GCA is excluded because both markers and the biopsy are negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Neither normal markers nor one negative biopsy rules GCA out; no single feature does.

options.text: Takayasu arteritis is the most likely diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Takayasu arteritis usually begins between 10 and 40, and the 2022 criteria require age 60 or under at diagnosis.

options.text: The biopsy result is invalid because ESR was normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Biopsy validity does not depend on the ESR; a normal ESR simply lowers, but does not remove, suspicion.

questions.stem: In suspected giant cell arteritis, how are an elevated ESR and CRP best described?

options.rationale: Correct. They are raised in most biopsy-proven cases (about 84–87%), but a meta-analysis found CRP only about 31% specific.
Incorrect. This describes temporal artery biopsy, not the inflammatory markers.
Incorrect. Raised markers occur in many other conditions; imaging and/or biopsy are needed.
Incorrect. Most patients have raised markers before treatment.

questions.stem: Which feature is an absolute entry requirement of the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for Takayasu arteritis?

options.text: Age 60 or under at diagnosis, with imaging evidence of vasculitis
options.rationale: Correct. The 2022 criteria require age ≤60 at diagnosis and imaging evidence of large-vessel vasculitis.
Incorrect. Age ≥50 is the entry rule for giant cell arteritis.
Incorrect. Temporal artery biopsy has no role in diagnosing Takayasu arteritis.
Incorrect. Female sex adds a point but is not required; men can have Takayasu arteritis.

claims.text: GCA age ≥50 (peak 70–79, highest in Scandinavia); TAK onset usually 10–40, 80–90% women, more prevalent in Asia; 2022 entry rules (GCA ≥50; TAK ≤60 plus imaging; 1990 TAK onset ≤40).

ESR 84.1% and CRP 86.9% sensitive for positive biopsy; 4% both normal without glucocorticoid use (10.2% including treated patients); CRP ~87% sensitive, ~31% specific; no single feature rules GCA in or out.

TAB highly specific but insensitive (false negatives up to 61% vs clinical diagnosis); GCA focal and segmental; >1 cm; within 2 weeks of glucocorticoids; contralateral biopsy or imaging if negative; ultrasound more sensitive; TAB has no role in TAK.
Arterial inflammation found in clinically inactive TAK; about one third without raised markers at presentation.

Reviewer’s “44% of quiet Takayasu have active arteritis on biopsy”; “up to 15%” TAB false-negative rate; “never stop steroids for a negative biopsy”; Scandinavian incidence >20/100,000; “Scandinavian whites”.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; the 15% figure is contradicted by a higher bound in Duftner 2018.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 54 Hit 7 and Trap 4 give temporal artery biopsy “up to a 15% false-negative rate”. Duftner 2018 (EULAR imaging review) reports false negatives in up to 61% of patients compared with a clinical diagnosis; the rate depends on the reference standard and population. The lesson teaches that false negatives are common and cites the source figure (register flag rv-gca-tab-false-negative-rate).

Ch. 54 Hit 7 and Trap 4 say 4% of biopsy-confirmed GCA cases have both ESR and CRP normal. In Kermani 2012 the 4% (7 of 177) applies to patients not taking glucocorticoids; 18 patients (10.2%) had both normal when those already on glucocorticoids are included. The lesson states the untreated qualifier (register flag rv-gca-normal-markers-steroids).

Ch. 54 Hit 15 separates Takayasu (<50) from GCA (>50). The 2022 ACR/EULAR Takayasu criteria use age ≤60 at diagnosis as an entry rule (the 1990 criteria used onset ≤40), so a 50–60-year-old can be classified as Takayasu; age cut-offs are classification rules, not diagnostic tests (register flag rv-takayasu-age-cutoff).
